##There are no missing values in gender, ethnicity_1, or ethnicity_2. The gender counts are very similar (14,452 Male; 14,948 Female). White participants are the largest category in both ethnicity variables.
##I will Keep ethnicity_2 because it retains the separate Asian category (3,284 participants), whereas ethnicity_1 combines this group into Other. It therefore preserves more information.

  
#Exercise 3
##My colleague’s plot shows raw body weight, which makes comparisons across participants difficult because they start at very different baseline weights. It also uses many colours and a long numeric legend, creating visual clutter without making individual trajectories easier to follow. The title is also missing, the axis labels are vague, and there is no visual reference for each participant’s baseline weight.

##A clearer approach is to calculate each participant’s change in weight from week 0. Every participant will therefore start at zero; negative values indicate weight loss and positive values indicate weight gain. Faceting gives every participant a separate panel, avoiding overlapping lines and eliminating the need for an unreadable colour legend. Keeping the same y-axis scale across panels also allows direct comparison of the magnitude of change

```{r}
## Import the diet dataset
diet <- read_csv("diet.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)

## Extract each participant's baseline weight at week 0
baseline <- diet |>
  filter(Week == 0) |>
  select(Participant, baseline_weight = Weight)

## Calculate change in weight from baseline
diet_change <- diet |>
  left_join(baseline, by = "Participant") |>
  mutate(
    change_from_baseline = Weight - baseline_weight,
    Participant = factor(Participant)
  )
```
 
  
```{r}
### Improved figure
plot_diet <- ggplot(
  diet_change,
  aes(x = Week, y = change_from_baseline, group = Participant)
) +
  geom_hline(
    yintercept = 0,
    colour = "grey40",
    linetype = "dashed",
    linewidth = 0.6
  ) +
  geom_line(
    colour = "#0072B2",
    linewidth = 0.7
  ) +
  geom_point(
    colour = "#0072B2",
    size = 1.4
  ) +
  facet_wrap(~ Participant, ncol = 4) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 16, by = 4)) +
  labs(
    title = "Change in Participant Weight During the Diet Study",
    subtitle = "Each participant's weight change is measured relative to their week 0 baseline",
    x = "Week of diet study",
    y = "Change in weight from baseline",
    caption = "Values below zero indicate weight loss; the dashed line represents baseline."
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    strip.text = element_text(face = "bold"),
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    panel.grid.minor = element_blank()
  )

plot_diet
```


#Exercise 4
```{r}
## Average available SBP readings for each participant
nhanes$average_sbp <- rowMeans(
  nhanes[, c(
    "systolic_bp_1", "systolic_bp_2",
    "systolic_bp_3", "systolic_bp_4"
  )],
  na.rm = TRUE
)

## rowMeans returns NaN when all readings are missing
nhanes$average_sbp[is.nan(nhanes$average_sbp)] <- NA_real_
```


```{r}
## Keep the final analytic sample
final_sample <- nhanes |>
  filter(
    !is.na(age),
    !is.na(gender),
    !is.na(average_sbp)
  ) |>
  mutate(
    gender = factor(gender, levels = c("Male", "Female")),
    age_cat = factor(
      age_cat,
      levels = c("0-17", "18-24", "25-39", "40-59", "60+")
    ),
    sbp_category = case_when(
      average_sbp < 120 ~ "Normal",
      average_sbp < 130 ~ "Elevated",
      average_sbp < 140 ~ "Stage 1 hypertension",
      average_sbp >= 140 ~ "Stage 2 hypertension"
    ),
    sbp_category = factor(
      sbp_category,
      levels = c(
        "Normal",
        "Elevated",
        "Stage 1 hypertension",
        "Stage 2 hypertension"
      )
    )
  )
```


```{r}
# Report the sample-size change
tibble(
  original_sample = nrow(nhanes),
  final_sample = nrow(final_sample),
  excluded = nrow(nhanes) - nrow(final_sample)
)

###importing my saved age distribution from exercise 2
knitr::include_graphics("figures/age_distribution.png") 

###create the equivalent plot for the final sample
plot_age_final <- ggplot(final_sample, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(
    binwidth = 5,
    boundary = 0,
    fill = "#00BFC4",
    colour = "white"
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "Age Distribution in the Final SBP Analysis Sample",
    x = "Age (years)",
    y = "Number of participants"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

plot_age_final
```

```{r}
### Required final faceted visualization
plot_sbp_age_gender <- ggplot(
  final_sample,
  aes(x = age_cat, fill = sbp_category)
) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill", colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ gender) +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format()) +
  scale_fill_manual(
    values = c(
      "Normal" = "#009E73",
      "Elevated" = "#F0E442",
      "Stage 1 hypertension" = "#E69F00",
      "Stage 2 hypertension" = "#D55E00"
    )
  ) +
  labs(
    title = "SBP Categories Across Age Groups and Gender",
    subtitle = "Final analytic sample",
    x = "Age group (years)",
    y = "Percentage of participants",
    fill = "Average SBP category"
  ) +
  theme_classic() +
  theme(
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold"),
    axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 30, hjust = 1),
    legend.position = "bottom"
  )

plot_sbp_age_gender
```


##The original NHANES dataset included `r nrow(nhanes)` participants. After excluding participants with missing age, gender, or average SBP, the final analytic sample included `r nrow(final_sample)` participants; `r nrow(nhanes) - nrow(final_sample)` participants were excluded.

##Comparison of the original and final age-distribution plots indicates whether the removal of missing observations materially changed the age composition of the sample.

##The final faceted figure shows how average SBP categories vary across age groups and between genders.
